title: Dex and the Downward Dash
markdown:
Dex was an invention tester. His job was to poke, prod, and play with wonderfully wacky contraptions. His workshop was a glorious mess of whirring gears, blinking lights, and funny springs. Machines that knitted socks all by themselves. Contraptions that polished shoes with a puff of air. A gizmo that sorted jellybeans by colour. Always beside him: Biscuit, a terrier mix whose ears flopped in opposite directions, forever surprised. His tail wagged like a hummingbird whenever Dex was near. A helpful bark. A hopeful wag.

One sunny morning Dex was tightening a tiny silver screw on a self-folding laundry machine that promised to sort socks with a cheerful whizz and pop. Clink! The screwdriver, no bigger than his pinky, slipped. It tumbled, spinning, down, down, down, and disappeared under a pile of colourful blankets with a tiny thud.

“Oh, bother.” His mop of unruly ginger hair seemed to droop.

Dr Hale ambled in, spectacles on the very end of her nose, a twinkle in her kind eyes, a bright red beanbag in her hands. “Good morning, Dex!” Warm as cocoa. She tossed the beanbag in a perfect arc. Whoosh! Down it tumbled, plop at his feet among the dust bunnies.

They all go down, thought Dex, watching it rest.

Hale picked up a smooth round ball the colour of a summer sky and rolled it along the workbench. Thump-thump-thump. It bumped merrily to the edge, rolled off, bounced, and came to rest near the fallen screwdriver.

“Every single thing,” Dex said, head tilted until ginger hair tickled his shoulder. “The screwdriver, the beanbag, the ball. They all go down. Why don’t they go up? Or float away like a balloon?”

Hale never just told you, like a grumpy teacher. “Ah, but here’s the thing, Dex. Let’s see for ourselves.”

“The Downward Dash!” Dex clapped. Biscuit sprang from under a workbench, tail a blur, a little woof of excitement.

Hale gathered oddities from around the workshop with the air of someone laying a feast. A fluffy white feather, so light it might dance away on a whisper of wind. A shiny metal spoon that reflected the lights like a tiny mirror. A soft woolly mitten, perfect for a chilly day. A bright yellow rubber duck, already looking cheerful, as if it knew about bouncing.

Dex carefully held the feather. The little barbs tickled his fingers. “Ready?” he whispered, leaning in. He let it go. Fluff-fluff-fluff. It drifted in a gentle wavy pattern, but always, always downwards, landing softly on the floorboards. The shiny spoon clanged, a sharp bright sound. The woolly mitten made a soft thump and vanished into a pile of colourful yarn. And the rubber duck? Boing! Boing! Boing! Great enthusiasm. Each bounce closer to the ground, until it settled with a happy little bob.

They all go down.

“It’s like an invisible string,” Dex mused, while Biscuit chased his tail in a dizzying circle — and even that tail, Dex noted, kept heading toward the floor.

Hale’s spectacles glinted. “Let’s try something more structured.” A sturdy board, propped as a ramp. A small heavy grey stone at the top. Whoosh — rumble to the bottom. A lighter bouncy ball. Boing-boing — down too, a little slower in the air, still pulled to the end.

“Heavy or light, fluffy or solid. They all get pulled downwards. Always towards the ground.”

A click in Dex’s head, the sound he made when a puzzle sat down. Not clumsy falling. A constant pull toward Earth.

“It’s gravity! Gravity pulls everything down!” He looked at Biscuit, who was trying to catch a leaf drifting in the window. “Even you feel it when you jump.”

Hale nodded. “It keeps our feet on the floor, our houses from floating away, the world steady. A constant friendly pull. Tiny pebble to biggest mountain.”

Dex scooped Biscuit, who showered his chin with slobbery licks. “So falling isn’t just being clumsy. It’s gravity doing its job.”

Now: the screwdriver. Small. Heavy. Gravity’s favourite kind of hiding. Low, under the blankets. Dex lifted the familiar soft weight of them, fold by fold, Biscuit supervising with a nose that believed in thoroughness. There, nestled deep within the folds, as if it had always meant to demonstrate the lesson: the tiny silver screwdriver. He held it up. It did not float. Biscuit woofed, which also did not float.

The sun dipped, orange and pink and deep purple. Biscuit’s tail thumped the floorboards, which did not float away. Dex set the screwdriver back in its dish, which also did not float away, and wondered what else might be quietly pulling — a leaf, a sock, a star. They all go down. Except the questions, which kept going up.
characters: Dex (an invention tester), Biscuit (a dog), Hale (a scientist)
